newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Maize Board may be scrapped by 1997/98.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Maize Board may be scrapped by 1997/98.

text.p: South Africa's Maize Board will be dissolved and withdraw from the export market by the start of 1997/98 (May-April) if the industry can agree a blueprint for a future marketing system by then.

Board general manager Leon du Plessis told Reuters a rough timetable for the closing of the state-owned Maize Board had been drawn up following new agricultural legislation that required the dismantling of all control boards.

"The maize industry at the Maize Advisory Committee during its meeting in August took a decision that by the end of November they would like a preliminary blueprint on the table that everyone can agree with in principle as to what the future marketing system, if any, will look like," du Plessis said.
"If everything goes according to plan that would mean that by April 30, 1997 the Maize Board will be dissolved," he said.
Asked if the board's involvement in the export market would cease then, he said, "It should come to an end for the simple reason that there will be no Maize Board anymore."
Du Plessis, however, cautioned that if the industry could not reach consensus on a new marketing dispensation the board would not fold before the 1997/98 season.
"I must stress that there is no finality...There are still a lot of discussions between all the role players," he said.
Although the Maize Board withdrew from intervention in the domestic market in May 1995, it remained active, alongside private traders, in the export market where it fixes a floor price.

Du Plessis said if the industry agreed on any new marketing structures for 1997, they would most likely be non-compulsory. "And if there are no structures it will be a free-for-all on the export market as well as on the domestic market."

Parliament last month passed the Marketing of Agricultural Products Bill, which sets a 13-month timetable for the dismantling of remaining farming control boards and requires industries to manage their affairs on a market-related basis.
Agriculture and Land Minister Derek Hanekom has on several occasions committed himself to the deregulation of the country's farming industry.
